sets.title: Redis protocol, one command per round trip
sets.tool: 3 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections
sets.pin: servers on one core, clients on 20 others
sets.note: Each server on one pinned core, every row at a full core: the rate is one core divided by the cost of an operation. SET and GET draw their keys at random from about a million, as a cache's clients spread them. At depth 1 that cost is mostly the kernel's per-message price, which all three pay alike, so the differences are small and the ranges wide; this VM halts idle vCPUs and every wakeup of a client costs the server a VM exit, which moves a server that answers each command with its own write more than one that batches.

sets.title: Redis protocol, 100 commands per message (pipelined)
sets.tool: 3 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections
sets.pin: servers on one core, clients on 20 others
sets.note: The per-message price divided by a hundred: what remains is parsing and executing commands, where the servers differ. SET and GET draw their keys at random from about a million, more than a core's caches hold, so each lookup waits on memory; SADD, HSET and ZADD put random members into one big collection each.

sets.title: Pipelined, one key
sets.tool: 3 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections
sets.pin: servers on one core, clients on 20 others
sets.note: The same commands on one key, which stays in the core's cache: the easy case for every cache, kept to show parsing and executing alone.

sets.title: Four cores, a cluster-aware client
sets.tool: 3 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections, 100 commands a message
sets.pin: socketley as four shards and Redis Cluster as four masters, each shard or master pinned to one of the same four cores; five redis-benchmark --cluster processes on 20 others
sets.note: SET and GET draw their keys at random from 1,048,576, 64 behind each of the 16,384 slot tags, preloaded so every GET finds its key (the hit rate is counted every pass). Every shard's mesh counters are read around every timed run: no command crossed between shards in any pass, so the client sent each to its owner. redis-benchmark --cluster's threads spin while they wait, so its client cores are no reading of headroom.

sets.title: Four cores, a plain client at one address
sets.tool: 3 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections, 100 commands a message
sets.pin: socketley as four shards on one port and Valkey with four I/O threads, on the same four cores; five redis-benchmark processes on 20 others
sets.note: SET and GET draw their keys at random from 1,048,576, three in four of them owned by another shard than the one a connection landed on: socketley carries those over its shard mesh, many commands a frame. LPUSH to ZADD name one key, which one shard owns, so socketley runs those on one of its four cores (see the cores column) and Valkey on its four I/O threads.

sets.title: WebSocket: echo and a chat room's fan-out
sets.tool: srvgen (Go), 4 s a run, every answer checked

rows.name: echo, 64 B messages, 256 connections, one in flight each
room fan-out: 1 sender to 100 receivers, 64 B
room fan-out: 1 sender to 1,000 receivers, 64 B

sets.pin: each server on one core (ws and uWebSockets.js under Node 24), srvgen on 20 others
sets.note: The same logic in each: an echo, and a room that a receiver enters by sending "join", with one sender's messages counted at every receiver. socketley runs it in Lua (join_group/group_send) and, as "no script", on its built-in relay; ws loops over the room with send(), uWebSockets.js publishes to a topic. Both socketley and uWebSockets.js build a room's frame once; socketley writes each receiver's share of a turn in one send, and uWebSockets.js corks its writes.

sets.title: TCP line protocol, answered by a handler
sets.tool: srvgen (Go), 4 s a run, every answer checked

rows.name: line echo, 64 B, 256 connections, one in flight each
line echo, 64 B, 64 connections, 16 pipelined each

sets.pin: each server on one core, srvgen on 20 others
sets.note: Every line is answered with itself by a handler: on socketley a Lua on_client_messages, handed a read's lines in one call and answering them with one self.send; on Node's net a function over the read's lines, written with one write a read; in Go a goroutine with bufio. With one line in flight the kernel's per-message cost dominates; 16 pipelined lines show each server's own per-line work, where a script with on_client_message, a call and a string a line, makes about 3.2 million a second.

sets.title: HTTP: static files and a fixed answer
sets.tool: wrk 8 threads, 4 s a run

rows.name: 1 KiB file, a connection per request, 64 at once
fixed answer (Lua handler / nginx return), keep-alive

sets.pin: each server on one core, wrk on 20 others
sets.note: socketley --http dir --http-cache against nginx with one worker, sendfile, open_file_cache and access logs off. Files are .txt: socketley adds a WebSocket script to every .html it serves, by design. The fixed answer is a Lua on_http_request on socketley and a return 200 on nginx, which runs no script at all. Read the 1 KiB keep-alive row with this machine in mind: nginx answers each request with its own write and wakeup, and on this VM waking a halted vCPU costs an exit, which costs a server that does that more than one that batches. A single unpublished pass on another VM (16 cores) read 1.85× for the same row. The kernel keeps at most 2,048 connections in TIME-WAIT for every arm (net.ipv4.tcp_max_tw_buckets, 131,072 by default), so a pass with a connection per request does not wait out the closed connections of the one before.

sets.title: HTTP on four cores
sets.tool: wrk 16 threads, 4 s a run

rows.name: 1 KiB file, a connection per request, 64 at once
fixed answer (Lua handler / nginx return), keep-alive

sets.pin: socketley as four shards and nginx with four workers, each pinned to one of the same four cores; wrk (16 threads) on 20 others
sets.note: The same rows as the one-core set, the same wrk for both. socketley spends about twice the CPU a request here that it does on one core, and most of that is the client, not the shards: wrk's threads each hold connections on all four shards, and waking a thread from another core is an interrupt the server's core pays for on loopback, a VM exit on this VM. With one wrk per quarter of the connections, four shards cost about 15% more a request than four separate one-core servers. A client on another machine costs neither. The kernel keeps at most 2,048 connections in TIME-WAIT for every arm (net.ipv4.tcp_max_tw_buckets, 131,072 by default), so a pass with a connection per request does not wait out the closed connections of the one before.

sets.tool: dnsperf 8 threads, 32 sockets, 4 s a run, zone of 10000 names
sets.pin: each server one worker on one core, dnsperf on 20 others
sets.note: Queries answered per second of server CPU (rate ÷ cores), because NSD and Knot do not fill their cores at a window of 500 outstanding queries, and with more they drop UDP from their default socket buffers and dnsperf waits out each loss. socketley runs with --rrl 0 --proxy none: its response rate limit, on by default, would throttle one client host, and NSD and Knot have none by default. 90% of queries find a name, 10% are NXDOMAIN.

sets.pin: each broker on one core, mqbench on 20 others
sets.note: MQTT 3.1.1, 64-byte payloads; Mosquitto with persistence off and unbounded queues, socketley --anonymous --session-queue 100000. A QoS 0 fan-out delivery costs Mosquitto about 2 µs of CPU, one write each; socketley coalesces the writes to a subscriber, which is the whole of the fan-out difference. sets.title: S3 over HTTP, SigV4
sets.tool: s3gen (Go, one process, a request in flight per connection), 4s a run, SigV4 over plain HTTP, PUT bodies aws-chunked and signed

rows.name: PUT 4 KiB, 64 connections, into an empty store

sets.pin: both servers on the same four cores (socketley as four shards), s3gen on 20 others
sets.note: MinIO single node, single drive; both on tmpfs, so the comparison is the servers' work and not a disk. MinIO is a Go server that limits itself on one core, hence four for both. s3gen signs every request with SigV4 as warp does (PUTs as signed aws-chunked bodies) and checks every answer's status, length and ETag; from 64 connections both servers fill their four cores. The 4 KiB rows read 2,500 objects, which socketley keeps as in-memory copies; the 50,000-object row reads past them, where every GET opens its file as MinIO's always do. The PUT row starts both servers afresh on empty storage for every pass, because MinIO reclaims deleted objects in the background and its puts slow while it does.

sets.title: OpenID Connect provider
sets.tool: idpgen, 4s a run, 200 accounts

rows.name: sign-in: authorization code with a password, 16 clients

sets.pin: both on the same four cores (socketley as four shards; Keycloak with its PostgreSQL), idpgen and wrk on 20 others
sets.note: 200 accounts. A sign-in is the authorization code flow with PKCE and a password, so it also compares the password hashes each uses by default: scrypt here, PBKDF2 in Keycloak. Keycloak's CPU includes PostgreSQL's. Refresh and userinfo come from four idpgen processes and JWKS from wrk, with as many clients as fill socketley's four cores; refresh stays near the same rate from 256 to 512 clients, bound by the durable write of each rotated token family through shard 0. Sign-ins come four at a time from each of four addresses: socketley refuses a fifth from one address while four are being checked, and four connections alone may land on two of its four shards, which would measure where the kernel put them. Both are warmed with sign-ins before the passes until a 5 s run gains under 3% on the best before it: Keycloak's JIT compiles the flow over its first half minute, from about 100 to 190 sign-ins a second.

connect: 200 TLS connections, each a full verified handshake
held: 200 idle connections, memory per connection
held: 10,000 idle connections, memory per connection

sets.pin: every client arm on one core, the Go target (clientgen) on four others
sets.note: Every client on the same one core, the target (a Go program) on four others with headroom: every row records the target's cores, and none used all four. socketley is one client runtime holding every connection (--connections N) with its Lua on_message as the handler; the others are one process with the same logic. Every count is taken at the target: a consumer's count must equal the lines sent, every request's size is checked, and a round trip is the interval between one connection's requests as the target sees them. The firehose rows are bound by the client's core, and every line differs (each carries its index). socketley's script reads them with on_read, walking a view of the read buffer with view:lines(), which makes no string, as Go's ReadSlice hands out a slice of its buffer; Node and Python make a string or a bytes object per line. Written with on_message instead, a Lua string per line, the 64 B row makes about 12.7 million lines a second, and with on_messages, one string per read, about 52 million. Over TLS the 64 B row is bound by the target, whose one goroutine encrypting the stream uses a whole core while socketley's runtime decrypts at about four fifths of its own; the target's cores beside the row say so. Connecting is that one runtime dialling all of them, as the others dial from one process; the memory row is socketley's daemon and the runtime's process together, by proportional set size, divided by the connections, so at 200 it is mostly the two processes' fixed cost. One runtime per connection instead, each made with socketley create ... -s from a shell loop, is a process each: 386 created and connected a second, 243 with TLS, and 1,546 KiB each held.
